pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 91: Planted: 12 seeds. Forgiven: 1 (not by me).*

I cancelled the park trip. Yusuf stared at me with his missing front teeth, waiting for an explanation. I handed him a sandwich, and he stopped asking.

The Summer Room was a graveyard of green. I pulled the dead stalks, and they snapped with a dry crack like the brittle ends of old bread crusts. I buried them in the soil, pressing the earth down with my knees. Theo sat on the bench, his knees pulled up, watching dust motes dance in the light. He did not help, but he did not need to; he was just there, which was more than I had been.

Gherkin moved between the rows. He was slow, but he was everywhere. He stopped near a dead tomato plant and looked at me, letting out a low, rumbling sound that felt like a sigh from the bottom of a well.

"Mm," he said.

It sounded disappointed. I picked up another stalk, my hands shaking because I wanted to fix it, to make it green again right now. But the earth was dry and hard, and the plants were gone. I could not bring them back. I could only make room for new ones.

"Mm," Gherkin said again, softer this time.

I kept pulling.
pages.image: Sana, in a denim jacket, kneels in a dry garden bed pulling up brown plant stalks, her face tight with effort; Theo, a boy in a beanie, sits on a wooden bench behind her watching, and a mossy tortoise peeks out from the leaf litter.

pages.text:
Twelve seeds sat in my pocket, heavy with promise, but I wanted the green back before the light failed, so I dumped them onto the dirt and started digging holes with frantic, scraping speed.

"Stop."

Gherkin’s head rose. His eyes were flat and dark.

"One a day," he said.

"No," I snapped. "The garden is dying. I can't wait. I don't have time."

He blinked, a process that took a long time, like an old dial-up connection loading.

"The garden is not dying," he said. "It is resting. One at a time is the only speed there is. You cannot buy time, Sana. You can only spend it."

I dropped the seeds back into the dirt and picked up just one, a bean, then dug a small hole and put the seed in, my hands finally still. I looked at the lemon tree by the wall, brown and brittle, and my throat tightened.

"I let it die," I said aloud, my voice sounding thin and cracked, like a dry piece of toast. "Because I wanted to be liked more than I wanted to be dependable."

The air changed, and a single yellow leaf dropped from the lemon tree, landing on the dirt with a soft thud, then, right beside it, a tiny green bud pushed out from a branch, small and stubborn and new.
pages.image: Sana holds a single bean seed in her hand, looking down at a small hole in the dirt; a large tortoise watches her intently; behind them, a lemon tree branch shows a single small green bud emerging next to a fallen yellow leaf.

pages.text:
Theo stood, brushing dirt from his jeans. His eyes moved from the new bud to my face.

"Grandma says you can kill a plant two ways," he said. "Starve it. Or love it only when it is easy."

He picked at a loose thread on his hoodie. The fabric frayed under his thumb.

"She said that to me when I was small," he continued, his voice dropping. "I thought she meant don't water it too much. Like, not enough."

He looked at the brown, brittle leaves. Then at the single green bud.

"I think she meant you have to show up when it is quiet. When nobody is watching."

He sat back down on the bench. He looked at the hedge, not at me.

"It is the best thing she ever told me. I just didn't get it until this week."

I looked at the bud. It was small. It was there because I had spoken the truth. I had not fixed the garden. I had just admitted where I had failed. And that was enough to start.
pages.image: Theo, wearing a beanie and a hoodie, sits on a garden bench looking at a hedge; Sana stands nearby holding a seed, listening; a tortoise is visible in the background near a lemon tree branch with a single green bud.

pages.text:
I could not sleep. The flat smelled of old bread and dust, and Baba and Yusuf were asleep. I lay on my back staring at the ceiling, watching the clock tick through midnight, then one, then two.

My chest felt hot. I put on my shoes, skipping the coat. The air was cool, but my impatience was not. I took the stairs, counting every single step because the rhythm kept me grounded. Ninety-two steps down. Then out to the loading bay.

The fence was cold against my knees as I crawled through the gap. Under the moonlight, the dead plants in the Summer Room looked silver and brittle. I grabbed the heavy watering can from the porch and filled it at the tap.

I poured the water over the roots, the new seed, and the dead leaves. I did not stop. I went back for more. One can. Then two. Then ten. My arms began to shake as water dripped down my wrists, but I kept going.

I was not doing it because I had to. I was doing it because the roots were dry, and I was there, and that was what mattered.
pages.image: Sana, in pajamas and shoes, carries a heavy metal watering can through a moonlit garden path toward a row of dead plants, her face determined; the silver light of the moon highlights the dry earth and her silhouette.

pages.text:
I finished the forty-second can, my arms having long since surrendered to gravity, so I let go of the metal handle. It clanged against the stone with a sound exactly like a dropped set of keys, startling me in the quiet.

My hair was loose, and my glasses were fogged over, blurring the moonlight into a soft, useless glow. My legs felt like they had been turned into warm, wobbly jelly. I walked back toward the fence, ready to crawl out, when I saw a light.

Mr. Osei was standing by the gate, his blue overalls dark in the night, his ring of keys jingling softly as he shifted his weight. He did not say anything, just watching me. I did not say anything either, just stood there holding the empty can.

Then he stepped aside, making room for me to pass. As I walked by, he spoke, his voice low and smooth, sounding like the hum of the bench in the Spring Room.

"Someone's been watering," he said.

I stopped and looked at him.

"Yes," I said.

He nodded, neither smiling nor frowning, just giving a slow, thoughtful nod.

"Good," he said.

He turned and walked toward the caretaker's office, the door opening to spill light onto the path. He stepped inside, and the door closed.

I stood in the dark, holding the empty watering can, trying to work out if I had just been thanked. I think I had.
pages.image: Sana stands in a moonlit garden holding an empty watering can, looking at Mr. Osei, a tall man in blue overalls with a ring of keys, who stands by a fence gate; a warm light glows from a nearby office window in the background.
